title: Which movies are examples of Style over Substance?

Style over Substance has always felt like a dumb kneejerk reaction to movies that operate more as mood pieces, hell I've even seen some psychos who thought Apocalypse Now was style over substance & one of my favorite movies ever 2019s Ad Astra has this complaint levied at it all the time, many neglect the fact that sometimes there is substance in style. Agreed. Style IS substance

Unpopular opinion: style over substance is a saying used by unintuitive people who can’t really be present for film. It’s a tool used by critics to devalue entertaining films or even worse to devalue abstract films. The critic foists his neurosis on a film for not regurgitating his own ideologies.

Saltburn, it relied too much on the style, and the soundtrack being cool that it didn’t end up being a good movie. I was an extra on the film and had an amazing time but I couldn’t even bring myself to say it was good

Agreed, which is funny because at least to me movies (& art in general) that focus on atmosphere & are more suggestive than concrete are incredibly engaging & it's why I've watched 1982's Blade Runner a million times & will watch it a million more times. Narrative heavy movies are great but there is so much talent in making a movie that communicate just as much through cinematography and tone as they might through a traditional narrative or dialogue.

Musicals immediately come to mind, to some degree.

Baz Luhrmann's *Moulin Rouge*, although in this case I might argue that style *becomes* substance.

Spielberg's remake of *West Side Story* could be considered a good example of style over substance.
[removed]

One could say Tron: Legacy is style over substance. But I tend to grade films on the curve. The plot is fine, but nothing revolutionary. The film sets out to immerse us as viewers into a world unlike our own. Tron 2 is definitely a feast for the eyes and ears and in that regard I’d say it’s mission accomplished.

What makes Michael Bay movies dumb isn’t that they are “style over substance”, it’s that the style is clanky and meh.

Johnnie To is style over substance, but they’re so originally conceived and beautifully executed that you never stop to ask yourself, *Wait, what is going in here, again?*

Michael Bay’s style is never engaging enough to make you suspend your frontal lobes and just enjoy the sensation, like a Johnnie To movie can.
This for me is “style is the substance”

I get the arguments people are making for why this phrase encourages bad faith criticism. Style is part of the subtance of film. Artistic vision has inherent value. Visual Art: it's in the name.

But we all know Baz Luhrmann is style over substance, and I say that as a person that loves Moulin Rouge.

I think I don't like this train of thought simply because I think human nature has an ability to overanalyze anything that they like and tend to overlook things from films they don't. 

That being said, I don't think Independence Day could really be thought of it as anything but a a wacky mixtape of War of the Worlds and Star Wars,  and I think in that regard is very successful at being a high octane popcorn movie.

I think if there was more emphasis on three dimensionality and depth, that particular film wouldn't operate as well. 

So I think a lot of what makes a movie work are things that are uniquely filmic... whether the dog makes it through the alien bombardment or combating alien technology with basic malware, whenever it aims for something truly dramatic, it's more of a gasp for the next action beat. 

But it has Jeff Goldblum and Will Smith and Bill Pullman, so I'm not going to complain too much, I like the film.

>we all know Baz Luhrmann is style over substance

No, no we don't. I personally think there's quite a bit going on in his movies, especially compared to a lot of "serious" Hollywood films.

The most visually captivating films of all time suck you into the story. You're not only sitting on your couch as an observer "watching the film", it feels like you're there within the world the movie creates, experiencing the events unfold with the characters. That amplifies every emotion a scene is trying to convey. That's why visuals are so important in film, at least for me.

Sorry there's a mouse in my pocket.

You're shifting the goalposts there. If I criticise a film for being 'style over substance', I'm not criticising it for being too subtle or for not featuring a solid narrative. More likely I'm saying I feel like I just watched a wonderful production design and maybe some cool camera stylings, but not much more. There's a difference.

I disagree on the outright rejection of "style over substance", as there can be films with substantial or insubstantial style. A movie like *Sucker Punch* I'd consider one of the latter, as a collection of basically interchangeable fantasies that mostly exist 'to look cool' and don't work toward, possibly even against, the movie's 'point'. *Oblivion* is another highly aesthetic action movie, but its style is substantial: how it looks means something, you can't swap out its images and retain the same implications.

"Spielberg's remake of *West Side Story* could be considered a good example of style over substance." 

No, it could not. First, because it's not a remake, and second, and most important, because the style is motivated by the themes and the internal condition of its characters. By that same logic, someone could say *The Red Shoes* is style over substance.
